stem: What is the subshell in which the last electron of the first element in the 6th period enters ?
solution: The 6th period begins by filling the last electron in the shell with \(n = 6\). The lowest energy subshell of any shell is 's'. Therefore the last electron of the first element in the 6th period enters the subshell '6s'.

stem: How many elements are present in the 6th period? Explain.
solution: The 6th period begins by filling the last electron in the subshell '6s' and ends by completing the subshell '6p'. Therefore, the sixth period has the subshells filled in increasing order of energy as \(6s < 4f < 5d < 6p\). The electron capacities of these subshells are 2, 14, 10 and 6, respectively. Therefore, the total number of elements in the 6th period are \(2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32\).

stem:
Outer electronic configurations of a few elements are given below. Explain them and identify the period, group and block in the periodic table to which they belong.

\({}_{2}\mathrm{He} : 1s^2\), \({}_{54}\mathrm{Xe} : 5s^2 5p^6\), \({}_{16}\mathrm{S} : 3s^2 3p^4\), \({}_{79}\mathrm{Au} : 6s^1 5d^{10}\)
solution:
**\({}_{2}\mathrm{He} : 1s^2\)**
Here \(n = 1\). Therefore, \({}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) belongs to the 1st period. The shell \(n = 1\) has only one subshell, namely 1s. The outer electronic configuration \(1s^2\) of 'He' corresponds to the maximum capacity of 1s, the complete duplet. Therefore, He is placed at the end of the 1st period in the group 18 of inert gases, so 'He' belongs to p-block.

**\({}_{54}\mathrm{Xe} : 5s^2 5p^6\)**
Here \(n = 5\). Therefore, \({}_{54}\mathrm{Xe}\) belongs to the 5th period. The outer electronic configuration \(5s^2 5p^6\) corresponds to complete octet. Therefore \({}_{54}\mathrm{Xe}\) is placed in group 18 and belongs to p-block.

**\({}_{16}\mathrm{S} : 3s^2 3p^4\)**
Here \(n = 3\). Therefore, \({}_{16}\mathrm{S}\) belongs to the 3rd period. The 3p subshell in 'S' is partially filled and short of completion of octet by two electrons. Therefore 'S' belongs to \((18 - 2) = 16\)th group and p-block.

**\({}_{79}\mathrm{Au} : 6s^1 5d^{10}\)**
Here \(n = 6\). Therefore, 'Au' belongs to the 6th period. The sixth period begins with filling of electron into 6s and then into 5d orbital. The outer configuration of 'Au' : \(6s^1 5d^{10}\) implies that \((1 + 10) = 11\) electrons are filled in the outer orbitals to give 'Au'. Therefore 'Au' belongs to the group 11. As the last electron has entered 'd' orbital 'Au' belongs to the d-block.

stem: Chlorides of two metals are common laboratory chemicals and both are colourless. One of the metals reacts vigorously with water while the other reacts slowly. Place the two metals in the appropriate block in the periodic table. justify your answer.
solution:
Metals are present in all the four blocks of the periodic table. Salts of Metals in the f-block and p-block (except \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\)) are not common laboratory chemicals. Therefore, the choice is between s- and d-block. From the given properties their placement is done as shown below:

s-block: Metal that reacts vigorously with water

d-block: Metal that reacts slowly with water.

The colourless nature of the less reactive metal in the d-block implies that the inner d-subshell is completely filled.

stem: Identify the species having larger radius from the following pairs : (i) \(\mathrm{Na}\) and \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\), (ii) \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\)
solution:
(i) The nuclear charge is the same in \(\mathrm{Na}\) and \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\). But \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) has less number of electrons and less number of occupied shells (two shells in \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) while three shells in \(\mathrm{Na}\)). Therefore, radius of \(\mathrm{Na}\) is larger.

(ii) \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) are isoelectronic species. \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) has larger nuclear charge than \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) has larger radius.

stem: The first ionization enthalpy values of \(\mathrm{Si}\), \(\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) are 780, 1060 and 1255 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. Predict whether the first ionization enthalpy of \(\mathrm{S}\) will be closer to 1000 or 1200 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed page sets the element symbol Cl as 'C1' (a digit one for the letter l) in both the question and the solution, and the unit kJ mol-1 as 'kJ mo1-1' twice. Transcribed here as Cl and mol, which is what the chemistry requires; no value or conclusion is affected.]

As we move across the period 3 from left to right the elements \(\mathrm{Si}\), \(\mathrm{P}\), \(\mathrm{S}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\) come in a sequence. Their outer electronic configurations are \(3s^2 3p^2\), \(3s^2 3p^3\), \(3s^2 3p^4\) and \(3s^2 3p^5\) respectively and 'P' loses an electron from a singly occupied 3p orbital whereas 'S' loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital. Therefore, the first ionization enthalpy value of 'S' has to be lower than that of 'P'. Thus, first ionization enthalpy of 'S' would be less than 1060 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), and therefore, should be close to 1000 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and not 1200 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

stem:
Identify the element with more negative value of electron gain enthalpy from the following pairs. Justify.

(i) \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed page sets the element symbol Cl as 'C1' (a digit one for the letter l) in the question and as 'CI' (a capital I) at the start of the solution, before spelling it correctly later in the same paragraph. Transcribed here as Cl throughout; no value or conclusion is affected.]

(i) \(\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) belong to the same group of halogens with \(\mathrm{Br}\) having higher atomic number than \(\mathrm{Cl}\). As the atomic number increases down the group the effective nuclear charge decreases. The increased shielding effect of core electrons can be noticed. The electron has to be added to a farther shell, which releases less energy and thus electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative down the group. Therefore, \(\mathrm{Cl}\) has more negative electron gain enthalpy than \(\mathrm{Br}\).

(ii) \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) belong to the same second period, with \(\mathrm{F}\) having higher atomic number than \(\mathrm{O}\). As the atomic number increases across a period, atomic radius decreases, effective nuclear charge increases and electron can be added more easily. Therefore more energy is released with gain of an electron as we move to right in a period. Therefore, \(\mathrm{F}\) has more negative electron gain enthalpy.

stem: \(\mathrm{Ge}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\) belong to the groups 14, 16 and 17, respectively. Predict the empirical formulae of the compounds those can be formed by (i) \(\mathrm{Ge}\) and \(\mathrm{S}\), (i) \(\mathrm{Ge}\) and \(\mathrm{Br}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the question labels its two parts '(i)' and '(i)'; the second should read '(ii)', as the printed solution itself does. The two parts are the Ge-S compound and the Ge-Br compound, and no answer is affected.]

From the group number we understand that the general outer electronic configuration and number of valence electrons and valencies of the three elements are :

| Element | Group | Outer electronic configuration | Number of Valence electron | Valency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{Ge}\) | 14 | \(ns^2 np^2\) | 4 | 4 |
| \(\mathrm{S}\) | 16 | \(ns^2 np^4\) | 6 | \(8 - 6 = 2\) |
| \(\mathrm{Br}\) | 17 | \(ns^2 np^5\) | 7 | \(8 - 7 = 1\) |

(i) \(\mathrm{S}\) is more electronegative than \(\mathrm{Ge}\). Therefore, the empirical formula of the compound formed by these two elements is predicted by the method of cross multiplication of the valencies :

Element: \(\mathrm{Ge}\), \(\mathrm{S}\); Valency: 4, 2. Cross multiplication gives Formula: \(\mathrm{Ge_2S_4}\), and hence Empirical formula: \(\mathrm{GeS_2}\).

(ii) \(\mathrm{Br}\) is more electronegative than \(\mathrm{Ge}\). The empirical formula of the compound formed by these two elements in predicted by the method of cross multiplication of valencies :

Element: \(\mathrm{Ge}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\); Valency: 4, 1. Cross multiplication gives Formula: \(\mathrm{GeBr_4}\), and hence Empirical formula: \(\mathrm{GeBr_4}\).

stem: Write the chemical equations for reaction, if any, of (i) \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) and (ii) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) both. Correlate this with the position of \(\mathrm{Na}\) and \(\mathrm{Al}\) in the periodic table, and infer whether the oxides are basic, acidic or amphoteric.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed working sets NaCl as '2NaC1' (a digit one for the letter l), HCl as '6HCI' (a capital I), and the plus sign of the second aluminium equation as a circled-plus symbol. Transcribed here with the correct symbols; the equations balance as printed and no conclusion is affected.]

(i) \(\mathrm{Na_2O + 2HCl \longrightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{Na_2O + NaOH \longrightarrow}\) No reaction

As \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) reacts with an acid to form salt and water it is a basic oxide. This is because \(\mathrm{Na}\) is a reactive metal lying on the extreme left of the periodic table.

(ii) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 6HCl \longrightarrow 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \longrightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O}\)

As \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) reacts with an acid as well as base to form a salt and water. It is an amphoteric oxide. \(\mathrm{Al}\) is a moderately reactive element lying in the centre of main group elements in the periodic table.
